questions.q: State the three main functional categories of textile finishes based on the fabric property they modify, giving one example of a finish in each category.
questions.a: The three categories are: (1) Appearance-changing finishes – e.g., bleaching, calendering; (2) Texture-changing finishes – e.g., starching, sanforising; (3) Behaviour-changing finishes – e.g., water-repellent, flame-retardant, anti-shrink (sanforisation). A wrong answer that lists dyeing/printing as separate categories instead of sub-types of appearance finishes reveals confusion between colour application and the broader functional classification.

questions.q: Explain why a 100% polyester fabric cannot be dyed with direct dyes used for cotton, and name the dye class suitable for polyester.
questions.a: Polyester is hydrophobic with no polar groups for direct dyes (which rely on hydrogen bonding with cellulosic -OH groups) to attach; it requires disperse dyes that sublimate into the fibre at high temperature. A wrong answer citing "polyester is synthetic" without referencing hydrophobicity or dye-fibre affinity shows superficial understanding of dye-fibre chemistry.

questions.q: A designer wants a floral motif with three colours on a silk sari. Recommend the most appropriate printing method and justify why roller printing would be unsuitable.
questions.a: Hand screen printing is most appropriate: it allows multiple colours with precise registration on delicate silk, and the low pressure avoids fabric distortion. Roller printing is unsuitable because its high-speed metal rollers exert excessive tension and heat, damaging silk's protein structure and causing dye migration. A wrong answer choosing block printing for "traditional look" ignores the need for fine multi-colour registration on a long sari length.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the durability and renewability of starching versus sanforisation, and explain which finish a consumer would prefer for a daily-wear cotton shirt.
questions.a: Starching is a renewable finish (washes out, needs reapplication) that adds stiffness and soil resistance; sanforisation is a durable mechanical pre-shrink finish (permanent, survives washing). For daily-wear cotton shirts, consumers prefer sanforisation because it eliminates shrinkage without changing hand-feel, whereas starching requires repeated effort and can cause discomfort. A wrong answer calling starching "durable" confuses temporary stiffening with permanent dimensional stability.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Dyeing at the fibre stage is always superior to fabric-stage dyeing because it gives better colour fastness." Provide two scenarios where fabric-stage dyeing is actually preferred.
questions.a: The statement is false. Fibre-stage dyeing gives excellent fastness but lacks flexibility: (1) For solid-colour fabrics with quick fashion turnover, fabric-stage dyeing allows rapid response to colour trends; (2) For blended fabrics (e.g., polyester/cotton), fabric-stage cross-dyeing creates unique two-tone effects impossible at fibre stage. A wrong answer agreeing with the statement ignores the commercial need for flexibility and blended-fabric effects.

questions.q: Design a finishing sequence for a grey wool fabric intended for winter coats that must be water-repellent, shrink-resistant, and have a smooth lustrous surface. List the finishes in order of application with chemical/mechanical justification for the sequence.
questions.a: Sequence: (1) Scouring (remove grease/impurities) → (2) Milling/felting (controlled shrinkage for density) → (3) Decatising (steam setting for dimensional stability) → (4) Water-repellent finish (fluorocarbon pad-dry-cure) → (5) Calendering (heat/pressure for lustre). Justification: Wet finishes first, then heat-setting, then chemical finish last to avoid wash-off; calendering last to lock in lustre. A poor answer omits scouring or applies water-repellent before decatising, risking uneven treatment.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Textile finishing is the series of treatments applied to fabric after loom-state production to enhance its appearance, texture, or performance for specific end-uses, including colour application (dyeing/printing) and functional ______ (water-repellent, flame-retardant, anti-shrink).
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a textile ______ in Jaipur creating a summer collection: you have grey cotton fabric from the loom that feels stiff, looks dull, and shrinks when washed.
What is Textile finishing? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Textile finishing is the series of treatments applied to fabric after loom-state production to enhance its appearance, texture, or performance for specific end-uses, including colour application (dyeing/printing) and functional modifications (water-repellent, flame-retardant, anti-shrink).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Textile finishing?
questions.a: Students believe "finishing" only means adding colour (dyeing/printing) and that all finishes are permanent.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to classify a given finishing treatment as routine/durable/renewable, appearance/texture/behaviour change, and identify the appropriate dyeing stage (fibre/yarn/fabric) and printing method for a specified design requirement, justifying each choice with fibre-specific reasoning.
